title: Homelessness in the US Fell the Most in More Than a Decade
summary:
After years of climbing to record-high levels, the homeless population in the United States dropped more than 6% in 2025. That amounts to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It is the second year in a row that homelessness has declined, following a smaller drop in 2024.

Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner announced the results of an annual count of people in communities around the country. "President Trump's actions to secure the border, get criminal illegals off our streets, and restore safety to our communities drove a historic decrease in homelessness," Turner said in a press release. The agency had not yet posted a detailed report.

A second independent analysis based on the same count, commissioned by the advocacy group National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline but credited different reasons. "It's good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working," said CEO Ann Oliva.

Both analyses find there are still nearly 700,000 people in the US living in shelters or on the streets, significantly more than before the COVID-19 pandemic. The Trump administration cited its changes in immigration policy as a key factor in the decline. During the previous administration, New York, Chicago, Boston, and Denver all saw a surge in asylum seekers who turned up at homeless shelters. "That's also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently," said Devon Kurtz of the Cicero Institute, an administration ally on homelessness policy.

Kurtz also pointed to declines in cities like San Francisco, which is moving to support more sober-living options, housing that bans drugs and alcohol. But critics say that can send more people back to the street if they relapse, which is common. The administration argues that requiring people to be drug-free would help more people achieve recovery, and it wants to overhaul several billion dollars in homelessness spending and shift it toward short-term housing with mandated addiction and mental health treatment. So far, that plan has been blocked by courts.

The administration says the longstanding federal policy of getting people into permanent housing first, then offering voluntary treatment, has failed and is to blame for the pandemic spike in homelessness. But Oliva said programs that get people off the street without preconditions were a big part of the latest declines, especially among veterans. Homelessness among US veterans was down more than 7% last year, and has declined nearly 60% since 2010. By contrast, Oliva said more permanent housing is needed for people who have been homeless for a long time, and who are more likely to struggle with mental health problems and addiction. Unlike other groups, they saw a small uptick last year.

HUD also credited a crackdown on homeless encampments after the Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that cities can ban people from sleeping and camping in public places. Oliva said the analysis her group commissioned showed that cities with such bans "actually did worse than the national average." She noted the decline was broad and likely due to a number of factors, including softening rental markets in some places. Even though rents are still high, they are down from record peaks during the pandemic, which could slow the flow of newly unhoused people. There were also declines in places hit by major weather disasters, like western North Carolina and Hawaii, where relief efforts reached unhoused people as well.
why_it_matters: Nearly 700,000 people are still without a home, so a drop in the numbers matters — but the disagreement over why it happened will shape how billions of dollars are spent on housing and help in the years ahead.

background_read: Homelessness means living without a home of your own, in a shelter, a car, or on the street.
Each year, communities across the country count how many people are in that situation, so the government can see whether the number is rising or falling.

Housing programs try to help in different ways: some give people a home first and offer help with health or addiction afterwards, while others ask people to take part in treatment before or alongside housing.
The count is a snapshot, and different groups can look at the same numbers and disagree about what caused them to change.

OPEN QUESTION: Which approach will bring the number down further: housing people first, or requiring treatment first?
